concepts.def: The fundamental units — including the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin and mole — from which other units are derived.
Unpredictable scatter in repeated readings; its effect is reduced by repeating measurements and averaging.
A consistent offset affecting every reading the same way, such as a zero error; not reduced by repetition.
The interval around a measured value within which the true value is expected to lie, e.g. ±0.5 mm.
The absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value, multiplied by 100.
The smallest change in a quantity that a measuring instrument can detect or display.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Measurements & Errors — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Measurements & Errors brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Measurements & Errors.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a systematic error?
options: A balance reading 0.02 g with nothing on it (zero error).
Scatter in repeated timings due to reaction time.
Misreading a scale once by accident.
A draught varying readings randomly.

mcqs.q: Taking repeat readings and averaging reduces the effect of:
options: Zero errors
A parallax offset present identically in every reading
Random errors
Systematic errors

mcqs.q: A length is measured as 50.0 mm ± 0.5 mm. The percentage uncertainty is:
Which of the following is an SI base unit?
options: The newton
The volt
The kelvin
The joule

mcqs.q: Does taking repeat readings reduce systematic error?
options: No — accuracy only applies to digital instruments.
Yes — repeats remove the need for calibration.
Yes — averaging removes all types of error.
No — repetition reduces random error; a systematic offset remains in every reading.

mcqs.q: Are precision and accuracy the same thing?
options: No — resolution has no connection to uncertainty at all.
No — accuracy only applies to digital instruments.
Yes — a precise result is automatically accurate.
No — precision is how closely repeated values agree with each other; accuracy is closeness to the true value.

mcqs.q: Does an instrument with finer resolution guarantee a smaller overall uncertainty?
options: Yes — the uncertainty equals the instrument's resolution and nothing else.
No — resolution has no connection to uncertainty at all.
No — overall uncertainty also depends on technique, calibration and random effects in the measurement.
No — accuracy only applies to digital instruments.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Percentage uncertainty”?
options: The absolute uncertainty divided by the measured value, multiplied by 100.
Unpredictable scatter in repeated readings; its effect is reduced by repeating measurements and averaging.
The smallest change in a quantity that a measuring instrument can detect or display.
A consistent offset affecting every reading the same way, such as a zero error; not reduced by repetition.
